summary: This repository contains the anonymised aggregated data, Python analysis code, and supporting documentation for the Bayesian hierarchical analysis of time to antibiotic administration in the PALOH-UK study. PALOH-UK was a prospective, multicentre implementation study evaluating the introduction of rapid point-of-care MT-RNR1 genotyping into routine neonatal care across 14 neonatal units in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland between March 2025 and June 2026. The study assessed whether incorporating pharmacogenetic testing into neonatal admission pathways affected the timely administration of antibiotics. The repository provides the data and code used to estimate changes in time to antibiotic administration following implementation, accounting for differences between neonatal units, uncertainty in baseline measurements, and repeated post-implementation audits. The primary analysis included 863 admissions with antibiotic administration times greater than zero and up to 120 minutes. Sensitivity analyses extended the upper threshold to 180 minutes (948 admissions) and removed the upper threshold entirely (990 admissions). The repository includes the analysis scripts, input datasets, model specifications, reproducibility instructions, and outputs from the primary and sensitivity analyses, including convergence diagnostics. Associated manuscript: McDermott JH et al. National implementation of point-of-care MT-RNR1 testing to prevent aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity in newborn infants: a prospective multicentre study.   Study registration: ISRCTN10216938. Funding: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), Invention for Innovation (i4i) Programme (NIHR208090).
title: PALOH-UK: Data and code for Bayesian analysis of time to antibiotic administration following implementation of point-of-care MT-RNR1 testing

summary: Open data on how Baton Rouge, Louisiana weather stresses automotive paint (UV, heat, humidity and rain), and on how often it allows a ceramic coating to be applied and cured. It includes a 12-city U.S. comparison and the 1950–2025 record of 90°F days at Baton Rouge Metro Airport. Headline findings: Baton Rouge averaged 111 days at or above 90°F and 117 days with a peak UV index of 8 or more each year from 2016 to 2025. 59% of all hours were at 80% relative humidity or higher, and 21 "hot-sun rain days" a year brought rain on a 90°F, very-high-UV day. Days at 90°F+ have risen about 2.9 per decade since 1950 (Sen's slope; Mann-Kendall p = 0.014). Airport hourly observations show 165 days a year (2016–2024) when a coating could be applied at 50–86°F and 80% humidity or less with no rain for the next 24 hours. That falls to about 2 days in July and 2 in August, against about 21 in October. On a combined paint-stress score, Baton Rouge ranks 3rd of 12 U.S. metros, after Tampa and Miami. Files: daily Baton Rouge records 2006–2025 (station and NASA POWER model values, with cure-window flags), the 12-metro benchmark, monthly and annual profiles, the 1950–2025 heat record, a threshold sensitivity table, EPA AQI context, stats.json with every headline figure and validation result, a methods PDF with the data dictionary, charts, and the Python code that rebuilds everything from public sources. Sources: NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily and ISD-Lite; NASA LaRC POWER Project (hourly API); U.S. EPA AirData. Report: https://www.immaculatecarwash.com/guides/ceramic-coating-weather-study-baton-rouge
title: Baton Rouge Car Paint and Ceramic Coating Weather Dataset, 2006–2025
Replication Materials: When Machine Speed Stops Mattering

summary: In this article, we propose ContactFlowFilter, a novel approach for contact estimation that determines the number of active contacts, their locations, and the associated force vectors. We consider a robot manipulator equipped with joint torque sensors and a base force/torque sensor; such a proprioceptive-only setup presents a challenging inverse problem characterized by (i) multi-modality from non-unique solutions, (ii) temporal dependencies in state evolution, and (iii) discrete contact events involving contact addition/removal. Existing approaches, such as particle filters (PFs) and learning-based methods, often struggle to address these challenges simultaneously. To overcome this, ContactFlowFilter integrates a generative model into the PF framework. The recursive structure of the PF captures temporal dependencies, while the flow matching model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events. Extensive validation in both simulation and real-world experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method. In real-world settings, ContactFlowFilter achieves the lowest dissimilarity from the target distribution, with errors of only 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm for single- and dual-contact scenarios, respectively, while operating at 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms.
title: Mixture of Flow Matching and Particle Filter for Proprioception-Based Online Contact Estimation

summary: Malicious actors frequently obfuscate their code to hinder investigative reverse engineering efforts. Among the most formidable techniques is virtual machine (VM) obfuscation: programs are translated into bytecode for a custom VM, often with a randomized virtual instruction set and distributed alongside a corresponding interpreter. Manual analysis and deobfuscation scale poorly due to the complexity of VM obfuscation and the diversification techniques that render each VM and interpreter unique. Existing methods primarily focus on simplifying execution traces and identifying virtual execution boundaries. However, comparatively little attention has been given to recovering higher-level program semantics from VM-obfuscated code. To address this gap, we propose VMSpec, a novel decompiler-based approach that automates the construction of VM processor specifications, enabling existing, well-known decompilers to analyze the VM-obfuscated code. We evaluate our prototype of VMSpec on 147 programs from an established obfuscation benchmark, comprising hash functions, standard algorithms, and randomized functions, obfuscated with different configurations of the Tigress and Code Virtualizer obfuscators. To demonstrate real-world applicability, we additionally include six domain generation algorithms stemming from real-world malware. VMSpec completely strips VM-obfuscation from nearly all obfuscated samples, producing output comparable to Ghidra's decompilation of the original code. Furthermore, it is the first method capable of reconstructing the complete program behavior of VM-obfuscated programs with infinite, input-dependent paths and recursive calls.
title: VMSpec: A Decompiler-based Approach against Virtual Machine Obfuscation

summary: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.
title: Unlocking Spatial Grounding in Flow-Matching Models via SNR Tuning

summary: We consider the problem of Bayesian estimation associated to inverse problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). In most cases of practical interest, one must use numerical solvers to implement computational methods based on Monte Carlo methods. This inevitably leads to an adaptation of multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods to reduce computational efforts to achieve a pre-specified mean square error (MSE). MLMC is based on sampling coupled versions of Bayesian posteriors associated to increasingly precise numerical solves of the PDE. In this article we present a novel method to implement MLMC based upon sequential entropic optimal transport couplings learned with light Schrödinger bridges, and correct the transport with Metropolis--Hastings steps that preserve the pairing. We bound the mean square error associated to a version of our new estimation method and show, for an elliptic inverse problem, that to achieve a MSE of $\mathcal{O}(δ^2)$ ($δ>0$) one can have an optimal cost of $\mathcal{O}(δ^{-2})$. The results feature explicit bounds on the effect of the fitted transport and of the Metropolis--Hastings correction. From a numerical perspective, on elliptic, Darcy-flow and Navier-Stokes problems, the method reduces the variance of the most precise solver by a factor of five to ten and is faster than multilevel sequential Monte Carlo [arXiv:1503.07259] at tight accuracies.
title: Sequential Entropic Optimal Transport for Bayesian Inverse Problems via Multilevel Monte Carlo

summary: Nanoscale nonreciprocal elements are needed to control signal flow in scalable quantum technologies, but existing nonreciprocal components are often bulky. Here, we show that a strongly nonreciprocal current-voltage relation can arise entirely from coherent elastic scattering in a mesoscopic Rashba nanowire with gate-defined scatterers. We first identify the symmetry constraints that enforce reciprocal transmission in a phase coherent conductor even when inversion and time-reversal symmetry are broken. We then show how gates that are capacitively coupled to the leads, together with a magnetic scatterer or transverse subband mixing, can remove these constraints. In the weak-scattering regime, nonreciprocal conductance originates from interference between distinct backscattering paths. In the strong-scattering regime, nonreciprocity can be resonantly enhanced by the hybridization of the transmitting channel with bound states that arise from a higher transverse subband or spin-split band. In this regime, we find that a bias-induced change in the gate potentials of about one percent can produce an order-unity diode response, i.e., electrons are transmitted almost as in a clean wire for one bias polarity, whereas for the other polarity the current is strongly suppressed.
title: Quantum Interference Enhanced Rectification in Mesoscopic Nanowires

summary: Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state--gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $ΔΦ$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. These results identify a predictive--optimization gap: under the studied learner, a signal can describe outcome-relevant progress while failing to provide a reliably beneficial optimization direction.
title: The Predictive--Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play

summary: Magneto-mechanical resonators (MMRs) are a recently introduced sensor technology for tracking and sensing applications that enables effective miniaturization down to the millimeter regime. However, estimating sensor parameters such as position from raw signals remains computationally challenging, because it requires solving a nonlinear inverse problem with computationally demanding objective function evaluations. In this work, we show how a deep learning method can accelerate this process by directly learning the inverse mapping from the measured signals. We consider the localization problem as an example and show that a convolutional-transformer regressor trained on simulated data with recorded noise can generalize to experimental data. The method achieves a median Euclidean distance error of 7 mm, which is comparable to the size of the sensor and corresponds to 6% of the size of a single coil. These results suggest that deep learning is a promising approach for rapid estimation of MMR parameters.
title: Data-Driven Localization of Magneto-Mechanical Resonators from Time Signals

summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories

summary: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.
title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion

summary: Soliton pumping enables controlled transport of localized wave packets through the interplay between nonlinearity and band topology. Interactions between such wave packets provide an additional means to manipulate their localization and subsequent motion. Here, we investigate collisions of solitons in a driven bichromatic lattice, where solitons associated with bands of opposite Chern numbers are pumped toward one another. For intracomponent collisions, the soliton that dominates the collision survives as a localized outgoing wave packet, while the weaker one can lose its distinct localized identity. For intercomponent collisions, attractive interaction produces spatial locking, whereas repulsive interaction induces redistribution toward the lowest band and reverses the motion of the initially excited-band wave packet. Remarkably, for collisions between vector solitons with comparable initial intensities, the difference between their internal relative phases controls the collision outcome, favoring capture for in-phase preparation and re-separation for out-of-phase preparation. These results connect nonlinear scattering with subsequent topological pumping and identify initial intensity, intercomponent interaction, and relative phase as control parameters for manipulating localized transport within the same pumping protocol.
title: Collision Dynamics of Topologically Pumped Solitons

summary: Pyralysis (PYthon Radio Astronomy anaLYSis and Image Synthesis) is an open-source Python library for radio-interferometric simulation, gridding, and image reconstruction. Imaging is stated as an explicit optimization problem — chi-squared (and closure / bispectrum terms) plus regularizers you choose — solved with modern first-order methods (e.g. FISTA, L-BFGS, SDMM). It is not a black-box CLEAN imager.
title: Pyralysis
Reconstruction of the Neutrino Nature Based on the Great Tao Model and a Unified Explanation of Related Puzzles

summary: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.
title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong

summary: Generative recommenders replace the retrieve-then-rank cascade with a single model: beam search over semantic item identifiers performs retrieval, and the same likelihood performs ranking. We show that this shared score makes them forget long-tail items twice. In retrieval, beam search keeps identifier prefixes by the probability mass of their subtrees, so tail items are pruned early, and a wider beam admits few more of them. In ranking, the likelihood places tail items below head items even when they are admitted, so expanding retrieval alone brings little or no gain. Both failures reflect missing item-level memorization (i.e., direct recall of which items co-occur), which collaborative filtering provides and shared-prefix generation lacks. To this end, we propose CAPE (Co-occurrence-Aware Pool Expansion), a training-free plug-in that restores memorization at both stages: (i) a memorization channel retrieves co-occurrence-supported tail items outside the beam and scores them with the frozen generator, and (ii) memorization-calibrated ranking fuses the generator likelihood with co-occurrence evidence while keeping the generator's first item. Experiments with two generative backbones on product and music domains show that CAPE significantly improves long-tail accuracy over the backbones and over re-ranking baselines that share its candidates, preserves or improves overall accuracy, and adds a small fraction of the latency.
title: Generative Recommenders Forget the Long Tail: Restoring Memorization in Retrieval and Ranking

summary: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI

summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.
title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents

summary: Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.
title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits

Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.
title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits

summary: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development

summary: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.
title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents

summary: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing

summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.
title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems

summary: Reliable video perception over bandwidth-constrained wireless links requires transmitting information that the receiver cannot already recover from its evolving scene representation. This paper introduces WorldGT, a world-model-guided semantic packet transmission framework that prioritizes information according to its contribution to the receiver's perception. A shared feature-space world model predicts the receiver's scene state through affine motion compensation and learned residual displacement, while sender-side verification identifies reusable predictions. An acknowledgment-synchronized receiver twin estimates task-impact scores through two counterfactual evaluations, guiding packet selection and unequal error protection over LDPC-coded wireless channels. A compact 3-bit feature representation increases spatial coverage under stringent bandwidth constraints, while predictive fallback sustains perception during packet outages. Experiments on KITTI and VisDrone under Rayleigh fading and AWGN demonstrate substantial gains in low-SNR conditions. On KITTI at a 4.13% reference bandwidth budget, WorldGT achieves 47.5% J&F at 0 dB Rayleigh SNR, outperforming H.264 by 11.3 percentage points. Controlled ablations show that world-model prediction contributes up to 8.7 points under Rayleigh fading. Object-detection experiments further demonstrate the transferability of receiver-relative predictive transmission across visual perception tasks. These results establish world-model-guided, receiver-state-aware transmission as an effective approach to robust video perception under severe communication constraints.
title: Guess and Send: World-Model-Guided Semantic Packet Transmission for Robust Video Perception

summary: We consider the open-loop optimal control of a dynamical system whose state is described by a time-dependent matrix $X(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. Gradient-based optimization methods may incur substantial computational and memory costs, particularly for large-scale systems and fine temporal discretizations. To alleviate this computational burden, we develop a mathematical framework to use Dynamical Low Rank Approximations (DLRA) in optimal control problems. We study two distinct paradigms: the first one, called Optimize-then-Project (OtP), first derives the optimality system and then approximates both the state and adjoint equations using DLRA. The second one, called Project-then-Optimize (PtO), first replaces the state equation with its DLR approximation, and then derives the optimality conditions for the resulting optimization problem. The two approaches differ fundamentally concerning the role of the adjoint variable. In OtP, the adjoint variable evolves on the manifold of fixed rank matrices, whereas in PtO, the adjoint variable belongs to the tangent space to the fixed-rank manifold at the evolving state variable. This latter formulation leads to a covariant ODE describing the dynamics of the adjoint variable as the underlying tangent space evolves in time. For both approaches we establish rigorous error estimates for the approximated gradients, identifying how their accuracy depends on the low-rank approximations of initial and terminal conditions, the components of the state and adjoint vector fields normal to the relevant tangent spaces, the stability properties of the dynamics, and the manifold curvature. PtO further requires tailored time discretization strategies for the adjoint covariant ODE, which we show to be robust against small singular values of the state variable. To illustrate the framework, we apply these methods to the optimal control of a random parabolic PDE.
title: Dynamical low-rank approximations for the optimal control of matrix ODEs

summary: Training modern AI models has become increasingly expensive, and updating deployed models can alter their internal feature representations, affecting applications built upon them. In retrieval systems, such updates often require complete gallery re-indexing, a computationally expensive process at scale. Existing backward-compatibility methods enable direct comparison of representations from updated and earlier models, avoiding re-indexing. However, they typically require compatibility-specific training, learned mapping functions, or architectural modifications, and often depend explicitly on the previous model. We propose hyperspherical simplex representations derived from softmax outputs and logits for backward-compatible retrieval across independently trained models. They leverage the simplex structure induced by softmax cross-entropy training with one-hot labels as a common geometric reference across model updates. Since this reference depends on the number of classes, adding new ones expands the simplex, misaligning existing class prototypes with their earlier counterparts. We therefore derive a deterministic linear transformation to restore their alignment. Our theoretical analysis of the formal backward-compatibility definition identifies two geometric conditions under which its inequalities hold in expectation, assuming von Mises--Fisher class distributions with increasing concentration across updates. Aligned regular-simplex representations satisfy these conditions, providing a theoretical basis for the proposed representations under the stated assumptions. Without using additional compatibility-specific losses, learned mappings, or architectural modifications, the proposed representations achieve competitive results on standard compatibility benchmarks, including expanded class sets, more expressive architectures, and independently trained models from public repositories.
title: Hyperspherical Simplex Representations for Backward-Compatible Retrieval

summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have seen broad adoption, but their biases are still far less examined than those of standard LLMs, creating possible social harms when deployed in real-world settings. Prior efforts to extend bias analyses from LLMs into the multi-modal space either cover only a few bias categories or do not ensure that the groups being compared are clearly addressed by visual cues in the images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Melange, a wide-ranging synthetic visual benchmark covering seven categories for assessing social biases in MLLMs. It is grounded in the widely used language-only BBQ dataset (Bias Benchmark for Question Answering) from BigBench, carefully extending its constructed contexts via controlled generation of visual scenarios so the target attributes appear visually and clearly. To maximize reliability, our generated images pass through two stages of validation: automated screening using visual question answering (VQA) and subsequent manual inspection by human annotators. By systematically evaluating 23 open-source MLLMs across three matched evaluation settings---text-only, image-only, and image-with-context---Melange isolates the fairness effect of the input modality. Switching from text to vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average, a gap that varies by model family rather than by scale alone. A perception control confirms that this gap is not an artifact of visual comprehension: models identify the depicted attributes at 90--95\% accuracy yet still fail to abstain. When models do commit to a biased answer, polarity-aware stereotype alignment shows they choose the human-stereotypical response roughly three-quarters of the time.
title: Melange: A Synthetic Visual Bias Benchmark for Multi-modal Large Language Models

summary: Residual-based causal discovery assumes that each variable is generated from its parents and an independent noise source. It estimates this noise and tests its independence from candidate causes. For identifiable functions such as additive-noise models (ANMs) and the broader class of location-scale noise models (LSNMs), this principle identifies the causal direction, as only the causal model admits this independence. Existing LSNM methods rely on parametric assumptions to obtain standardized residuals, risking model misspecification. In contrast, the RESIT-framework allows for nonparametric estimation of residuals to iteratively identify sink nodes, but was proposed for ANMs. To close this gap, we propose Loscar, an extension of RESIT to LSNMs that estimates the conditional mean and scale via quantile regression, enabling pretrained tabular foundation models as plug-in estimators. We compare it with a feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) variant, which is consistent given suitable basis functions. Across bivariate and multivariate causal-discovery benchmarks, in-context quantile regression substantially outperforms FGLS with flexible function classes, particularly for multivariate causes.
title: Residual-Based Causal Discovery via Pretrained In-Context Quantile Regression

summary: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.
title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity

summary: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for multi-step reasoning, yet obtaining reliable process labels remains a central bottleneck. Existing approaches typically rely on human annotation, rollout-based estimation, or auxiliary verification. In this work, we explore a different source of process supervision natively exposed by Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: expert routing. We show that simple routing statistics provide an intrinsic process-confidence signal that is competitive with conventional output-logit confidence. Building on this observation, we construct routing confidence by combining overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation, and introduce RoCo-Rethink, which identifies the least confident reasoning step and selectively regenerates the subsequent trajectory. We further introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM. Across multiple MoE architectures and diverse reasoning tasks, both RoCo-Rethink and RoCo-PRM consistently outperform strong baselines, while RoCo-PRM transfers effectively across both model architectures and tasks. Our findings suggest that expert routing is more than a computational dispatch mechanism: it provides an architecture-native source of process supervision for reasoning.
title: A Strong MoE Is All You Need for Process Supervision

summary: In this work, we assess the recently introduced spin-adapted TDA for spin-flip-down excitations (XSF-TDA) [Mol. Phys. e2631735 (2026)] as a practical approach to this problem. Starting from a high-spin restricted open-shell Kohn--Sham reference, XSF-TDA generates spin-adapted low-spin roots arising from open--open (OO), core--open (CO), open--virtual (OV), and core--virtual (CV) types of spin-flip-down excitations. Across four application sets comprising 243 benchmark cases, XSF-TDA substantially reduces the systematic positive bias observed for TDA and unrestricted spin-flip TDA (USF-TDA). With the B3LYP functional, XSF-TDA reduces the equal-set-weighted macro-MAE relative to USF-TDA from 0.252 eV (0.158 eV) to 0.102~eV (0.056~eV) with the ALDA0 (multicollinear) kernel. Its accuracy is competitive with state-specific $Δ$DFT and quasiparticle-energy DFT (QE-DFT), while being able to provide deeper mechanistic insight through the response vector. In particular, spin-adapted CV configurations provide selected higher-excitation character that strengthens the OO--CV dynamical-spin-polarization channel, which preferentially stabilizes the singlet states. We also identify an INVEST emitter with appreciable OO--OV mixing, suggesting a possible additional contribution to singlet stabilization when the CV contribution is small. The XSF-TDA method therefore provides practical singlet--triplet gap predictions together with interpretable state analysis for the screening and mechanistic understanding of MR-TADF and INVEST emitters.
title: Spin-Adapted Spin-Flip Tamm-Dancoff Approximation (XSF-TDA) for Singlet-Triplet Gaps in MR-TADF and INVEST Emitters

summary: Suitability maps guide perennial-crop expansion but are rarely converted into units that planners can allocate, tested for robustness to analyst choices or checked against presence records. We assessed land suitability for macadamia ( Macadamia integrifolia ) in four provinces of northwestern Vietnam, where a national programme targets 75,000–95,000 ha by 2030, using twelve FAO-rated criteria weighted by fuzzy AHP under baseline and 2041–2070 climates (five CMIP6 models, two scenarios). We delineated plantable zones: contiguous blocks of at least 1000 ha that keep a suitability index of 0.75 or more in all eleven runs and lie outside forest-planning land on slopes of at most 20°. Before the minimum-area rule, this land forms more than 100,000 patches, and projected changes in suitable area changed sign at high thresholds. Delineation produced 89 zones covering 346,945 ha, whose location changed little across weight sets (Jaccard ≥ 0.78), largely because the exclusion masks fix where zones can lie. Of 88 presence records not used to set class limits, 69% lay within 3 km of a zone, against 39% of the region, also after spatial thinning; mask-only zones did as well, so the agreement reflects the masks and cannot test the index ranking. With no heat or drought criterion, warming relaxes the cold limit, but the best low-lying zones decline most. The zones cover 3.7–4.6 times the 2030 target, yet half their area carries tree cover, a quarter is cropland and grassland alone falls short of it, so land availability is the likely constraint (SDGs 15 and 2).
title: Climate-robust plantable zones for macadamia outside forest-planning land in northwestern Vietnam

summary: This archive contains the code used for the experiments of the paper "AICAT: an AI tool for hierarchical cell-type annotation" (Dailin Gan, Siyuan Zhang and Jun Li), as used for the revised manuscript (release v1.0.0-revision). Contents: code/Build_Agent holds AICAT as run for the benchmark of 238 samples, with preprocessing, the LLM evaluator and the organisation of results and figures. code/GPTCelltype holds the GPTCelltype runs. code/Revision holds the experiments and analyses added in the revision: ablation, comparison with CASSIA and ScType, marker perturbation, repeated runs, runtime and cost, blinded re-scoring, statistics, figures and tables. code/process_data holds early GTEx processing scripts. requirements.txt records the Python environment. See code/README.md for details. The processed data are available on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.16739980). The installable AICAT package is aicat-annotator (PyPI; https://github.com/RavenGan/AICAT). To run the code, set the environment variable OPENAI_API_KEY; no API key is stored in the code. The third-party ScType scripts and database (GPL-3.0) are not included; code/Revision/external/sctype/SOURCE.md gives the exact source and checksums.
title: AICAT: code for the benchmark and revision experiments

Do Sentinel-2 vegetation indices improve forecasts of Phenacoccus solenopsis on okra? A two-season retrospective benchmark study

summary: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents

summary: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model

summary: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.
title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing

summary: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models

summary: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.
title: Stochastic Pruning of the DPO Computation Graph: 1.4x Faster Training and Lower Peak Memory

summary: We are the first to give a certified rule for whether unseen data belong in a pretrained model's context or its weights, built on an exact law for their information value. That value, the code length saved on held-out queries, equals in expectation the bits stored about the query, plus a prior repair, minus a decoding loss, for any model, architecture, dataset and task. The law's ceilings certify the choice from one measurement, and an anytime-valid test makes it from held-out queries, with error controlled whenever it stops. Every certificate the ceilings issue on a trained transformer, TabPFN, an occupancy network and a stereo network is correct. The test picks TabPFN over XGBoost and a trained surrogate over an in-context learner on airfoil pressure, calls the better of GPT-2's cache and fine-tune in 61,948 of 64,000 query streams over 32 comparisons, and errs in at most 3.3% of null streams. The law also diagnoses when learning in context helps and when it does not. Deleting part of a context is held-out validation of that part in any model, and adding parts one at a time traces the learning curve in context: one patch that sees a shape feature cuts an occupancy network's code length there a hundredfold, while eight that miss it nearly double it, and one camera that sees the surface beats four in a stereo network. Ranked by this label-free valuation, a kriging learner's three best support cars beat four drawn at random, and on a yes-or-no claim the valuation recovers a published evidence adjudicator, with AUROC 0.91.
title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning

summary: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.
title: ChronoSynth: Constraint-Aware Question Synthesis over Temporal Knowledge Graphs

summary: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.
title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience

summary: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.
title: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling

summary: Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills. Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground. We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution. The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model. At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43-46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.
title: Compressing Onboard Language Models for Space Robots under a Behavioral-Fidelity Requirement

summary: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts

summary: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.
title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.
title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs

summary: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.
title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
