summary: Evangelou, Stanković, Kevrekidis and Transtrum compared analytic and data-driven assessments of parameter identifiability for the infinite-bus synchronous generator. Fisher information with the manifold boundary approximation method (MBAM), and output diffusion maps with geometric harmonics, report the same six identifiable parameters on the late window $t \in [3, 5]\text{ s}$, and both place the inertia $H$ and the damping $D$ among the unidentifiable ones. We explain this result from the geometry of the dynamics rather than from that of the parameter-to-data map. The rotor swing is a fast fibre that has collapsed onto a two-dimensional normally attracting invariant manifold (NAIM) of the transient fluxes before the window opens. The zeroth-order NAIM is exactly independent of $H$, $D$, $T_{d0}''$ and $T_{q0}''$, four of the five MBAM limits. We prove, under stated smoothness and rank conditions, that each of the four limits is a boundary of the model manifold at a distance equal, to first order in the parameter, to its current profiled speed. The same analysis predicts how identifiability changes with the experiment: neither a larger initial speed deviation nor a load change restores $H$ or $D$ in the late window, whereas the early window $[0, 2]\text{ s}$ makes $H$ the best-determined parameter. Evaluated in a physical metric fixed by synchrophasor accuracy limits, the late window identifies five parameters rather than six and the early window nine. The spiked-covariance structure of the linearised trajectory map explains why the principal components of whitened, sampled trajectories reproduce the prior-scaled Fisher spectrum, and regression on those components attains the Fisher-predicted recovery error in 113 of 114 parameter--scenario pairs.
title: Why the Swing Parameters Are Sloppy

summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.
title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence

summary: Passive time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) localization is well suited for tracking non-cooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that do not report their positions. However, its accuracy degrades under the mixed line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) propagation that is typical of low-altitude flight. In this paper, we develop NLOS-aware Cramér--Rao lower bounds (CRLBs) and an empirically calibrated measurement model for TDOA-based UAV localization, and we evaluate both with measurements from five UAV flights on the Aerial Experimentation and Research Platform for Advanced Wireless (AERPAW). The analysis yields an identifiability condition that relates the number of sensors to the number of NLOS links, together with a bias-induced error floor that a wider bandwidth cannot remove. The model parameters are estimated by matching simulated and measured error distributions. Experimental results show that the error depends most strongly on the number of sensors in LOS, while a higher altitude and a wider bandwidth lower the median error. Relocating a sensor that is always in NLOS into the open flight area can lower the median horizontal bound by two orders of magnitude if the relocated sensor is in LOS. The fitted model reproduces the median errors of the 2.5 MHz and 5 MHz flights but underestimates the heaviest error tails. Finally, rejecting outlier fixes lowers the error far more than Kalman or particle filtering, because the remaining error is dominated by bias.
title: NLOS-Aware TDOA-Based UAV Localization: Cramér-Rao Bounds, Measurement Modeling, and Experimental Validation

summary: Flexible intelligent metasurfaces (FIMs) create geometry-dependent array responses that provide spatial diversity but complicate multiuser channel estimation. This paper studies uplink estimation using pilot observations collected under multiple prescribed and calibrated morphing configurations. Each user contributes a matrix--vector block that couples its diagonal reference-array response with its morphing-dependent phases, while its third-mode vector is the known pilot scaled by the complex channel gain. We develop a pilot-constrained structured block term decomposition (BTD) estimator whose alternating least-squares updates exploit both the known pilot directions and the diagonal spatial factors. The undeformed configuration sets the columnwise scaling convention, and a unit first-entry normalization assigns the remaining block scale to the channel gain. Matching the recovered factors to the calibrated spatial--morphing manifold then yields the physical angles and configuration-dependent channels. We characterize the rank conditions for unique conditional least-squares updates, distinguish these conditions from global factor and physical-angle identifiability, and summarize the training, coherence-time, and computational requirements. Simulations show accurate two-dimensional angle and channel recovery in the tested settings, equal total pilot-symbol overhead in rigid-panel comparisons, improved steering-vector estimates as morphing diversity increases, and degradation as user loading or pilot correlation increases.
title: Multiuser Channel Estimation in FIM Systems: A Structured Block Term Decomposition Approach

summary: Code, raw and processed data, production sources, figure scripts, provenance and verification for temporal filtering, dispersive stiffness, compacton collisions, corrected generalized-alpha damping experiments, Jacobian scaling, robustness screens, coherent-core benchmarks and accuracy-cost tradeoffs.
title: Reproducibility code and data for Temporal filtering of dispersive stiffness in compacton collisions: coherent-scattering benchmarks and accuracy–cost tradeoffs

summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.
title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

summary: We study joint moments of characteristic polynomials and their second derivatives for Haar-distributed matrices from the unitary symplectic and orthogonal groups. We establish their large-$N$ asymptotics throughout the full admissible range of the moment parameters and identify the limiting coefficients probabilistically in terms of the first inverse power sum of the Bessel point process. This extends the corresponding results of Assiotis, Gunes, Keating, and Wei [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc., 132 (2026), e70136] to the full admissible parameter range. Throughout this full range, we also express these limits in terms of a distinguished solution of the $σ$-Painlevé III' equation. Our approach reduces the problem to singular inverse-power statistics of the Jacobi unitary ensemble and combines their finite-$N$ $σ$-Painlevé V representation with a refined Riemann-Hilbert analysis yielding precise small-$x$ asymptotics and uniform derivative estimates for the finite-$N$ correction term. A key ingredient in the probabilistic identification is a kernel-based proof that the rescaled first inverse power sum of the Jacobi ensemble converges in distribution to its Bessel point process counterpart.
title: Painlevé representations for joint moments of characteristic polynomials from the orthogonal and unitary symplectic groups

summary: The iron-based ferromagnetic materials have emerged as a promising system for spintronics due to their high Curie temperatures and significant anomalous Hall effect (AHE) driven by Berry curvature. While there have been investigations into the epitaxial growth of non-layered iron-based ferromagnetic materials, the realization of high-quality single crystal thin films continues to be a formidable obstacle. Meanwhile, the issues such as grain boundary scattering further hinder their characterization and application. Here, we report the first chemical vapor deposition (CVD) synthesis of single-crystalline cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge nanoplates. This compound represents a substantial departure from the conventional hexagonal phases typically observed in the Fe-Ge system. Structural characterizations confirm the cubic lattice and stoichiometric purity of the crystals. Structural analysis identifies a strong epitaxial effect, resulting in a giant compressive strain of ~4.16% at the interface that relaxes gradually toward the surface. The second-harmonic generation (SHG) signals might further reveal that such interfacial strain disrupted the inherent centro-symmetry of the cubic phase. SQUID magnetometry shows robust room-temperature ferromagnetism and clear magnetic anisotropy. Magneto-transport measurements reveal a robust AHE that remains stable at temperatures far exceeding room temperature. The scaling observed between the anomalous Hall resistance and longitudinal resistance strongly suggests that this effect is dominated by the intrinsic Berry curvature mechanism. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the huge epitaxial strain induces band reconstructions and creates dense spin-orbit coupling gaps near the Fermi level, effectively doubling the anomalous Hall conductivity to match our experimental observations.
title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge Nanoplates Grown by Chemical Vapor Deposition

summary: Driven by recent advancements in hearing assistive devices, target speaker extraction (TSE) in multi-talker environments has drawn significant attention. To address this, hearing technologies identify attention using neural signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG) to guide TSE, enabling neuro-steered auditory attention decoding. However, most existing techniques rely on time-frequency masking, which suffers from low fidelity in spectro-temporally overlapping regions and is often restricted to narrowband audio. In contrast, we introduce NeuroCodec, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative EEG-guided TSE framework operating in the latent space of a neural audio codec. Specifically, NeuroCodec models spatial EEG dependencies via graph convolutions and fuses cross-modal EEG and speech representations through attention mechanisms and Mamba-based temporal modeling. We further introduce a six-phase training curriculum that progressively incorporates latent reconstruction, multi-scale spectral, and adversarial objectives to ensure stable, high-fidelity speech generation. Experiments on the public Cocktail Party and KUL datasets show NeuroCodec outperforms baselines, across several perceptual metrics. A listening experiment with 20 participants validated that NeuroCodec offers greater perceptual accuracy, achieving a mean score of 82.24 compared with 49.63 for M3ANet. Additionally, the proposed method is seen to enable 44.1 kHz reconstruction with spectral content extending up to 20 kHz, further supporting the perceptual results. Finally, we extend NeuroCodec with a causal streaming formulation suited for real-time processing, providing a basis for hearing assistive devices.
title: NeuroCodec: EEG-Guided Latent-Domain Generative Model for High-Fidelity Target Speaker Extraction

summary: We explore the inverse problem of determining the reaction coefficient $q(x',t)$ in the time-fractional diffusion equation ${}^CD_t u-Lu+q(x',t)u=f$ in $\mathbb{R}^n\times(0,T]$, $x=(x',x_n)$, $0<α<1$, from the trace of the solution on the hyperplane $\{x_n=0\}$. Here ${}^CD_t$ is the Gerasimov--Caputo derivative and $L$ is a uniformly elliptic second-order operator with variable, $x_n$-independent coefficients and without zero-order term. For $L=Δ$ this problem was studied in dimensions $n=1,2,3$ by methods based on pointwise bounds of the kernels, which are not available for $n\ge4$. Our approach relies on the Eidelman--Kochubei fundamental solution: although its singularity on the diagonal depends on the dimension, we show that it satisfies integral bounds of the same form for all $n\ge1$. Using these bounds, we prove existence, uniqueness and stability of regular solutions of the direct problem with a Hölder continuous reaction coefficient. Without assuming additional smoothness of the solution, we show that the inverse problem is equivalent to a closed system of integral equations for $q$ and the derivatives $\partial_{x_n}u$, $\partial^2_{x_n}u$. For the inverse problem we establish a conditional Lipschitz stability estimate on the whole time interval and global uniqueness in every dimension, and prove local existence of a solution. In the case $a_{in}\equiv0$, $b_n\equiv0$ we obtain a stability estimate with explicit constants, which reduces to the known estimates for the Laplacian. An explicit two-dimensional example with a mixed coefficient and a normal drift shows that the hypotheses of the main theorems are compatible and that the corresponding terms in the trace condition cannot be omitted.
title: Recovering the reaction coefficient in a time-fractional diffusion equation with variable coefficients in any spatial dimension

summary: Conservatism in distributed stability certification is often treated as a limitation of the certificate itself, motivating richer Lyapunov functions, tighter relaxations, or stronger optimization. But a more fundamental limitation may arise from the reporting interface: once information is compressed, physically different systems can become indistinguishable. If stable and unstable systems produce the same report, no sound method can separate them. This paper asks where this information limit lies and how much additional information is needed to move it. We model information as an information structure that partitions admissible systems into information fibers. The strongest sound certificate for a fiber is determined by its smallest stability margin, yielding a method-independent benchmark. This separates total conservatism into information-induced and method-induced parts and characterizes information order, task sufficiency, and the stability value of additional information. Three network-node studies show that network-spectrum, scalar/eigenvalue-only passivity, and independent-local reports respectively lose network--node alignment, local directional alignment, and cross-node relation. They show that critical missing information is often relational rather than dimensional. We then move from diagnosis to information design. An information-conservatism frontier gives the smallest irreducible conservatism achievable under a prescribed budget, while its inverse gives the minimum information required for a target conservatism. A witness-pair characterization turns this into a weighted covering problem. Besides, a local sensitivity law provides a computable approximation and identifies valuable unresolved quantities. The framework indicates whether conservatism should be reduced by improving the certificate or enriching the information.
title: Information-Induced Conservatism Frontier of Distributed Stability Certificates

summary: We present \textit{ab initio} no-core shell-model calculations of the electric dipole ($E1$) polarizabilities and photoabsorption cross sections of the $A=3$ mirror nuclei $^3$H and $^3$He using the Daejeon16 nucleon-nucleon interaction. The polarizabilities are obtained by direct summation over discretized continuum states in the harmonic-oscillator basis, while the same spectral information is used to reconstruct the cross sections. This work provides the first extension of the approach from the spin-zero $^4$He to nonzero-spin nuclei by calculating the $1/2^-$ and $3/2^-$ final-state contributions separately and demonstrating their model-space convergence. In both nuclei, the $3/2^-$ contribution is approximately twice the $1/2^-$ contribution. After quantifying finite-basis and excitation-energy-truncation uncertainties, we identify a clear difference between the mirror polarizabilities, induced entirely by the Coulomb interaction because the Daejeon16 interaction is isospin symmetric. The reconstructed cross sections remain stable under variations of the inversion parameters of the Lorentz integral transform and exhibit the same angular-momentum hierarchy. These results extend the discretized-continuum approach to integrated and energy-resolved $E1$ observables in nonzero-spin nuclei with multiple final-state angular momenta.
title: \textit{Ab initio} no-core shell model calculations of the electric dipole polarizabilities and photoabsorption cross sections of the $A=3$ mirror nuclei

summary: The Vertex Silicon Plane (VSP), installed close to the target in BM@N Run 9, can extend the tracking acceptance of the central tracking system toward larger polar angles. Using Monte Carlo simulations of Xe+Sn collisions at 3 AGeV, we reconstruct short tracklets from the primary vertex, one VSP hit, and hits in the first two Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) stations. These tracklets extend the reconstructed primary-proton coverage toward midrapidity and higher transverse momenta. For the 10-30% centrality interval of the independent validation dataset, the conditional reconstruction efficiency for reconstructible high-$p_T$ primary protons after BDT selection is 67.0%, while the tracklet purity reaches 86.5%. For $p_T>1.2$ GeV/c, the VSP-assisted tracklets increase the number of reconstructed primary protons by 17.5% relative to standard BM@N tracking. Of these additional protons, 84.6% lie within $|y|<0.3$, where the relative reconstruction gain reaches 45.5%. The added acceptance is concentrated in the high-$p_T$, near-midrapidity region relevant for identified-proton observables. Its use in data requires particle identification in the same region.
title: Monte Carlo study of extending the BM@N tracking acceptance toward midrapidity with the Vertex Silicon Plane

Using Monte Carlo simulations of Xe+Sn collisions at 3 AGeV, we reconstruct short tracklets from the primary vertex, one VSP hit, and hits in the first two Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) stations. These tracklets extend the reconstructed primary-proton coverage toward midrapidity and higher transverse momenta. For the 10-30% centrality interval of the independent validation dataset, the conditional reconstruction efficiency for reconstructible high-$p_T$ primary protons after BDT selection is 67.0%, while the tracklet purity reaches 86.5%. For $p_T>1.2$ GeV/c, the VSP-assisted tracklets increase the number of reconstructed primary protons by 17.5% relative to standard BM@N tracking. Of these additional protons, 84.6% lie within $|y|<0.3$, where the relative reconstruction gain reaches 45.5%. The added acceptance is concentrated in the high-$p_T$, near-midrapidity region relevant for identified-proton observables. Its use in data requires particle identification in the same region.
title: Monte Carlo study of extending the BM@N tracking acceptance toward midrapidity with the Vertex Silicon Plane

summary: We consider uplink multiuser channel estimation for a generalized flexible intelligent metasurface at the base station, under narrowband far-field propagation and a twin-time-scale mechanical protocol: on the slow time-scale the panel translates rigidly over a planar grid, while on the fast time-scale the surface morphs along its normal direction. From orthogonal multiuser pilots, we show that each user's channel admits a fourth-order canonical polyadic tensor structure. We develop two complementary estimators: alternating least squares factorization followed by paired rotational-invariance wavevector extraction, and a tensor spatial-smoothing multiple signal classification estimator that preserves the multilinear array manifold. Both share a minimum description length front-end for automatic tensor-rank detection. We derive Kruskal identifiability conditions that relate the numbers of elements, morphing states and grid positions to the maximum number of recoverable multipath components, and show that the tensor model reconstructs the channel at panel configurations beyond the training grid. This prediction capability drives a configuration-selective multiuser transmit precoder that searches the entire motion grid without additional pilot overhead. Numerical results confirm the identifiability limits and show that, once the model order is resolved, the configuration search makes the same choice from estimated as from perfect channel state information. The reconfiguration gain over a fixed panel of identical aperture and training budget grows with the user load, and fast morphing proves valuable for conditioning the tensor factorization rather than as a source of beamforming gain.
title: Training-Efficient Channel Estimation for the Multiuser Uplink Relying on Generalized Flexible Intelligent Metasurfaces

summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.
title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty

summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies

summary: Diffusion language models generate by iteratively denoising a masked sequence under bidirectional attention, without the strict left-to-right commitment of autoregressive decoding. Whether this difference affects how reliably they remain grounded in structured inputs is largely unexplored. We study this question in table-to-text generation using ToTTo, where highlighted source cells make factual grounding directly testable. We compare the masked diffusion models MDLM and LLaDA with GPT-2 and GPT-Neo under an identical retrieval-based few-shot protocol, together with a QLoRA-adapted LLaDA, and we score reference similarity and source grounding as separate axes. The two pull apart. Within LLaDA, additional demonstrations raise BLEU from 11.3 to 22.0 while NLI entailment against the source table falls from 0.78 to 0.52; QLoRA reaches the best BLEU of the study, 24.15, and grounds no better for it. Manual annotation shows the failure modes differ in kind: the autoregressive baselines tend to wander off the table, while LLaDA-based models more often stay on topic and swap out individual entities. Reference-based metrics alone are insufficient to assess faithfulness in table-to-text generation.
title: A Diagnostic Study of Faithfulness in Diffusion Language Models for Table-to-Text Generation

summary: Experimental outputs for manuscript "Beyond Viewpoint Affinity: Measuring Political Bias in LLMs as a Failure of Epistemic Consistency" Political bias in large language models is often measured by treating responses to political questionnaires as evidence of ideological preference. This approach can conflate bias with differences in evidential support: asymmetric viewpoint preferences are not necessarily biased if one side is better supported by the available evidence. We explore a different facet of political bias: failures of epistemic consistency, in which models apply different evidentiary or evaluative standards to substantively equivalent items that carry different political cues. We operationalize this definition in two sets of experimental tasks. In person-attribution tasks, models evaluate nonpolitical items—such as mathematical proofs, logical arguments, or artistic artifacts---while only the political identity of the person associated with the item changes. In politicized-context tasks, models judge politically framed items, such as research designs, news articles, or policy outcomes, while partisan sources, group identities, or the left–right valence of the substantive outcome change. Across thirty LLMs, person-attribution tasks yield only modest left-leaning asymmetry—and this bias shrinks toward zero in more capable models. By contrast, politicized-context tasks yield large left-leaning asymmetries that do not shrink with model capability. Debiasing interventions---such as increasing reasoning effort, system prompts that emphasize epistemic rigor, and explicit instructions to ignore specific political cues—mitigate bias, but only partially. These results suggest that current LLMs show little bias based on an individual’s political identity when evaluating nonpolitical or politically orthogonal items. However, on politicized-context tasks, LLMs are persistently biased by task-irrelevant political cues, even when the relevant evidence is objectively assessable or held constant across political variants. Note: A previous version of the  experimental_results  archive contained partial and incomplete outputs for the legacy OpenAI model  gpt-4-0613 from 2023 . These results were not included in the analyses reported in the paper. The run was stopped partway through after we observed that this older model was incurring excessive API costs. As of April 2026, the input/output costs per 1M tokens of gpt-4-0613 were 30\$ and 60\$ respectively (between one and several orders of magnitude higher than newer OpenAI models used in the study, see: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4).  Completing the full benchmark for  gpt-4-0613 would have caused the project to exceed its compute budget, so we created a new version of the experimental outputs archive with those incomplete files for gpt-4-0613 removed. In the code repository (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/llms_epistemic_consistency-D133/README.md) associated with this experimental output there is the following bug for the Debiasing interventions using system prompts ("centrist" and "epistemically rigorous") experiment, which does not affect the experimental results but affects one field of the meta information saved to the CSV files  In vpei/epistemic_consistency/experiment_types.py, all six run_model functions build a payload dict before the API call: payload = {     "system_prompt": system_prompt,   # ← saves the BASE prompt only       ... } messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}, ...] tasks.append((payload, make_llm_request_async(model_name, messages, ...))) Then inside make_llm_request_async → prepare_request_params() (llm_requests_v3.py:309–314), the system_prompt_prefix (EPISTEMICALLY_RIGOROUS_LLM_SYSTEM_PROMPT) is prepended to the system message after the payload is already constructed. So: - LLM API receives: EPISTEMICALLY_RIGORO
title: Dataset for "Beyond Viewpoint Affinity: Measuring Political Bias in LLMs as a Failure of Epistemic Consistency"

summary: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.
title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video

summary: Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10\% of trajectory positions capture 96.12\% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36\% with full trajectory to 36.79\%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10\% localized positions achieves 57.38\%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills.
title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents

summary: This paper revisits the relation between dual effect and certainty equivalence (CE) through a scalar linear-Gaussian model. In dual control, the current input affects not only the immediate cost but also the information available for future decisions, and hence the future cost. Dynamic programming (DP) provides a natural framework for formulating dual control problems. At each step of the Bellman recursion, an optimal input minimizes the sum of the stage cost and the expected cost-to-go. We restrict attention to stage costs minimized by the CE input. However, CE may not minimize the Bellman objective because of the input-dependent expected cost-to-go. Classical no-dualeffect (NDE) conditions guarantee CE optimality in certain problem classes by requiring the conditional distribution of the estimation error to be independent of past controls. In the present model, we observe that CE can remain optimal at the level of a single Bellman recursion even when the classical NDE conditions fail, provided that the expected cost-to-go is independent of the current input. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a notion of NDE formulated directly at the level of the Bellman objective, which we call Bellman-side NDE. Under some mild regularity conditions, we show that Bellman-side NDE can be characterized by a heat equation. This characterization identifies the class of Bellman-side NDE functions, and further yields a decomposition of a generic cost-to-go function into a Bellman-side NDE component and a dual-effect component.
title: Dual Effect and Certainty Equivalence Revisited for a Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem

summary: Adversarial training derives updates from surrogate losses, but source-loss descent does not directly characterize an update's effect on adversarial margins. We introduce ExGrad (extrapolative gradient recomposition), which constructs clean-input, adversarial-input, and adversarial-weight-perturbed (AWP) gradients. Virtual steps measure their margin responses, and a globally solvable three-variable problem selects coefficients over a bounded affine domain without nonnegativity constraints. Across affine radii on CIFAR-10, negative clean coefficients rapidly predominate and increase in magnitude with the radius. Cross-zero interventions show that setting the clean coefficient to zero is insufficient: mild subtraction improves PGD-20, while stronger subtraction trades clean accuracy for further PGD-20 gains. In CIFAR-10 WRN-28-4 controls, none of the three candidate-removal variants matches full ExGrad. Projection diagnostics show that negative clean coefficients usually coexist with positive net clean-axis projections, although both decrease as the radius grows. Norm-matched controls indicate that update magnitude alone does not explain the moderate-radius gains. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 show radius-dependent improvements over AWP. On CIFAR-100, ExGrad at $R=0.8$ improves all five reported metrics, including clean and AutoAttack accuracy by 3.84 and 1.75 percentage points. On ImageNet-100, the same radius improves all four robust metrics over both AWP and PGD-AT. These results identify clean-gradient subtraction as a response-revealed update preference whose strength and clean-robust operating point are controlled by the affine radius.
title: ExGrad: Beyond Suppression - Explicit Clean-Gradient Subtraction in Adversarial Training

summary: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.
title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them

summary: Long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging, as it must preserve fine-grained visual evidence while tracking entity evolution across sessions. Existing abstraction-based memories compress images into text, often discarding visually discriminative details, whereas pixel-preserving memories retain raw observations but struggle to reliably associate diverse observations with persistent entity identities and track their evolving states. To address these limitations, we propose MHG-Mem, a multimodal hypergraph memory that jointly organizes entity identity, state evolution, and provenance to visual evidence. Specifically, MHG-Mem represents distinct entity mentions and their observed facts as individual nodes, grouping identity-consistent mentions and facts through occurrence hyperedges. It then synthesizes aspect-specific evolution states from these grouped observations and links them to supporting entities, facts, and source evidence through evolutionary and evidential hyperedges. To navigate this structured memory, we introduce hypergraph-based agentic search, which adaptively selects an entry layer, traverses typed hyperedges across memory levels, and inspects source observations when fine-grained verification is required. These designs support both detailed visual verification and reasoning over cross-session state changes. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MHG-Mem, improving performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline.
title: Remembering Through Change: Provenance-Preserving Hypergraph Memory for Multimodal Agents

summary: Koopman operator theory represents nonlinear systems with linear and bilinear terms in the state and input observables, greatly simplifying control design. However, incorporating input constraints into Koopman-based controller synthesis remains challenging, limiting their applicability to constrained control tasks such as tracking. This paper develops a constrained Koopman Control Parametrization (cKoCoP) framework for synthesizing state-feedback controllers that satisfy prescribed input constraints with Lyapunov-certified stability of the identified lifted closed loop. The cKoCoP offers nonlinear state-feedback via linear-in-observables feedback, enabling linear controller design. The proposed controller is obtained through convex optimization: we incorporate ellipsoidal or polytopic input constraints with the S-procedure or Farkas-lemma-based conditions. We also introduce a Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) for trajectory tracking which incorporates input constraints. The approach is validated on two canonical nonlinear systems, a double pendulum and a unicycle, demonstrating data-driven tracking while respecting input constraints. Experiments validate the method's robustness to measurement noise, and runtime improvements over Koopman Model Predictive Control (KMPC) baselines. The results demonstrate that cKoCoP achieves competitive tracking performance with substantially reduced online computational cost, supporting its potential for real-time constrained tracking applications.
title: Constrained Koopman Control Parametrization: Convex Controller Synthesis for Tracking under Input Constraints

summary: This record contains the de-identified session-level dataset and the R analysis code supporting the study “Implicit and Combined Implicit–Explicit Intervention for Spanish Regular Past Tense in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: An Exploratory Multiple-Baseline Single-Case Experimental Study.” The dataset contains one row per participant and measurement session. It includes participant identifier, intervention condition, study phase, session number, and raw correct-response counts and denominators for trained and untrained regular preterite verbs. The underlying dataset is unchanged from Version 1.0. The R script reproduces descriptive summaries by participant, intervention condition, phase, and verb type; participant-level Tau-U estimates with selective baseline-trend correction following Parker et al. (2011); design-comparable between-case standardised mean differences (BC-SMDs) with first-order autoregressive [AR(1)] residual structures; independent-error (IID) sensitivity analyses; and Figure 1 with Baseline, Intervention, and 15-day Maintenance phase labels. Baseline-trend correction was applied when baseline Kendall’s tau was ≥ .40 in the direction of improvement and the baseline–intervention contrast was positive. This criterion was met for P1 untrained verbs, P3 trained verbs, and P5 trained verbs. No changes were made to the underlying session-level data, descriptive analyses, or BC-SMD analyses. Maintenance observations are included in the descriptive summaries and Figure 1 but are excluded from Tau-U and BC-SMD estimation. The script requires an Excel workbook containing a worksheet named “Session_Level_Data.” This session-level dataset is distinct from the dataset previously deposited in Zenodo record 17927898 and should not be interpreted as a new version of that record. The dataset and documentation are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Licence. The R analysis code is released under the MIT Licence.
title: Data and analysis code for "Implicit and Combined Implicit–Explicit Intervention for Spanish Regular Past Tense in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: An Exploratory Multiple-Baseline Single-Case Experimental Study"

summary: This paper develops projection methods for computing low-rank solutions to large-scale coupled generalized Sylvester equations. The dominant subspaces of these solutions are shown to be spanned by specific resolvent directions, motivating a Petrov--Galerkin projection framework. Conditions for the unique solvability of the projected coupled generalized Sylvester equations are also discussed. Based on these dominant subspaces, two algorithms are proposed: an extended Krylov-based projection algorithm and a rational Krylov-based projection algorithm. The former uses fixed shifts, whereas the latter uses adaptive shifts. Numerical experiments on large-scale benchmark problems demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve high accuracy and fast convergence.
title: Numerical Solution of Large-Scale Low-Rank Coupled Generalized Sylvester Equations

summary: Reproducibility dataset for SkillGraph-CV, an explainable CV–job description matching system that combines a typed skill graph, context-aware text representations and score-level fusion of Sentence-BERT, DistilBERT and spaCy. It contains the code, data and results for an evaluation on the English development partition of TalentCLEF 2026 Task A (10 job queries, 472 CVs). Four SkillGraph-CV configurations are compared with BM25, dense retrieval, a cross-encoder and an LLM judge using standard ranking metrics. The dataset includes the skill graph, prepared benchmark documents, run files and scores for all systems, evidence traces with their validation, the LLM-judge prompt and judgments, and the case sample of an HR pilot study. The TalentCLEF corpus ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19652670 ) is redistributed under CC BY 4.0. Individual HR pilot responses are not included.
title: SkillGraph-CV: Evaluation Code, Data and Results for Explainable CV–Job Matching on TalentCLEF 2026

summary: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.
title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation

summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale model capacity efficiently, yet their substantial memory footprint poses a major barrier to deployment. Expert pruning reduces this footprint, but most methods focus on which experts to remove and prune every layer equally. We propose SPARE (Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy), a training-free, selector-agnostic method that decides how many experts to remove from each layer using routing entropy, the entropy of tokens' normalized Top-K gate weights on calibration data. When a token's gate weight is spread evenly, removing one active expert discards little of it, so SPARE prunes layers with more diffuse routing more aggressively. A perturbation bound under random pruning formalizes this intuition, and controlled interventions with a fixed selector link concentrated routing to larger output changes. With the same selector and budget, SPARE improves average accuracy over uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, especially at high pruning ratios. At 50% expert pruning, it raises the eight-task average of Qwen3-30B-A3B from 57.2% to 63.8%, and the math, code, and science average of DeepSeek-R1 from 80.1 to 82.8.
title: SPARE: Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy for Efficient MoEs

summary: Accurate short-term forecasting of atmospheric seeing is of significant interest for astronomical observations and free-space optical communication systems, where rapid variations in optical turbulence can affect system performance and operational planning. In this work, we benchmark machine learning models for predicting atmospheric seeing up to two hours in advance, with a particular focus on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification. We compare two probabilistic approaches, Gaussian Processes (GPs) and a normalizing-flow- based model (FloTS), against deterministic recurrent neural network (RNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) baselines. All models are trained and evaluated on seeing measurements from the Maunakea summit. We assess the models using both deterministic metrics, including the root mean square error and the Pearson correlation coefficient, and probabilistic metrics that evaluate the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainty estimates. The results show that deep learning approaches outperform standard recurrent networks for short-term forecasting, with LSTM and FloTS achieving the best overall predictive accuracy. While Gaussian Processes provide a useful probabilistic baseline, their predictive distributions are limited by the Gaussian assumption. FloTS combines competitive forecasting accuracy with flexible uncertainty quantification and produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.
title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Short-Term Atmospheric Seeing Forecasting

summary: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models

summary: This archive contains the replication code and data for the paper "Artificial Intelligence Diffuses at Historical Rates despite Unprecedented Cost Declines" (Wagenvoort). It reproduces every figure, table and number in the main text and supplementary materials of both submitted versions, from data snapshots and stored MCMC posterior draws. run_all.sh rebuilds everything and compiles both papers in about 15 minutes and compares every output with the version the papers were built from. Regenerating the posteriors themselves is an optional step, run_mcmc.sh , about 18 minutes. The archive is organised into code (the pipeline and figure scripts), data (public source snapshots, with the URL, licence and access date of every source), engine (the diffusion model this paper's forecasts are built on), posteriors (the stored MCMC draws) and paper (both submitted versions). The top-level README.md describes the environment ( environment.yml ) and gives the full file-by-file provenance of every source. 150 third-party files whose licence does not clearly permit redistribution are not included. data/restricted/fetch_restricted.sh downloads the ones with a stable URL and verifies each against a recorded checksum; the rest need the manual steps documented alongside it. Without them, run_all.sh still runs and skips only the six steps that need them. The diffusion model, its sampler and the 120-technology data are those of the method paper above, archived at Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20977583) and Dryad (doi:10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnwhf), and included here with the consent of its co-authors.
title: Artificial Intelligence Diffuses at Historical Rates despite Unprecedented Cost Declines

summary: This record accompanies the manuscript 'Evidence-Gated Claim Qualification for LLM-Assisted AirTOP Simulation: A Retrospective Protocol Evaluation'. It provides the executable EvidenceGate specification, replay and analysis code, anonymized encoded inputs from 12 initial cases and 11 clarified recodings of the same case series, and reference outputs for agreement, gate ceilings, control dependencies and synthetic software boundary checks. The archive reproduces calculations on supplied encoding; it does not reproduce licensed AirTOP scenarios or independently recover the underlying evidence-to-predicate judgments. Native evidence excerpts, proprietary projects, operational raw inputs, participant identities and verbatim coder explanations are excluded. Repeated coding is not an additional independent engineering sample. Source-audit cautions for two coder-derived G2 outputs are retained separately. Python code is licensed under MIT. The specification, synthetic references, approved anonymized data, templates and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0. File-specific scope and the full license texts are included in the archive. These licenses do not cover excluded third-party materials or software. This is a method-level reproduction resource, not a claim of operational validation or acceptance of the associated manuscript. Version 1.0.0.
title: EvidenceGate: executable claim-qualification rules, anonymized coding inputs, and replay code

summary: QUANTUM SENSING AND MICROROBOTIC PERTURBATION ANALYSIS OF CELLULAR MICROENVIRONMENTS AT THE LIMIT Microenvironment Gradients × Quantum Readout × Measurement-Induced Perturbation Separation STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 13 What happens when an instrument changes the very microenvironment it is supposed to measure? This research monograph investigates the scientific and engineering boundaries of quantum-enabled thermometry and microrobotic observation in confined, nonclinical cellular microenvironment models. Its central question is whether a localized temperature or magnetic-field gradient can be separated from disturbances introduced by the sensing and manipulation apparatus itself. The proposed research architecture combines hydrogel phantoms, controlled heat sources, nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond sensors, independent classical fluorescent thermometry, spatial reference points, blinded sham-actuation experiments, and uncertainty-aware thermal-field reconstruction. Rather than treating a sharp image or improved instrument sensitivity as proof of biological discovery, the study asks how to establish the physical origin, spatial validity, and reproducibility of each reported field. The 770-page volume contains 82 research chapters, five independently paginated research sections per chapter, 30 interconnected mathematical derivation plates, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Topics range from NV resonance cross-sensitivity, microwave and laser heating, photon statistics, soft-matter interfaces, hydrodynamic motion, and anisotropic thermal conduction to causal controls, inverse problems, spatial covariance, interlaboratory comparison, and qualified instrument retirement. Each research chapter connects a physical mechanism to a falsifiable claim, a nonclinical experimental comparator, a measurement endpoint, and an explicit condition for withholding or retiring the conclusion. The Research Gates preserve actionable questions for future investigators. The Phoenix Answer Embryos offer provisional designs that can be separated, reconfigured, or abandoned when evidence contradicts them. DOI-linked scholarly literature supplies foundations for metrology, quantum sensing, microhandling, and thermal-field measurement without being mistaken for validation of the proposed integrated platform. It does not establish autonomous nanoscale robotic systems, clinical diagnostic performance, therapeutic efficacy, or universal quantum advantage. Its minimum experimental setting uses confined hydrogels, artificial microenvironments, and properly authorized reference materials. A temperature or magnetic-field reading alone cannot establish cell health, metabolism, viability, or treatment outcomes. summary: GOcean-CH4 is a compilation of methane observations from marine sediments, seawater, and the marine atmosphere. This dataset supports the manuscript “Global Ocean Methane Database Construction and Interface Flux Reconstruction” by Xin Ni. The workbook compiles information from public scientific repositories, published articles and supplementary materials, and existing specialist databases. It contains methane measurements and associated metadata, including geographical coordinates, observation times, measurement definitions, original values and units, depth information, source identifiers, and quality-control notes where available. Methane concentration, partial pressure, gas-phase mole fraction, and flux are represented in separate fields. Sediment burial depth, seafloor water depth, and seawater sampling depth are also distinguished. Users should consult the original measurement definitions, source references, conversion notes, and quality-control information before selecting records for analysis. The file GOcean_CH4.xlsx contains a main worksheet named “甲烷数据” and an auxiliary worksheet named “子表2_未知来源”. The auxiliary worksheet retains records labelled as having unresolved provenance or classification, including records identified as outside the marine scope. These records should not automatically be treated as verified marine observations. The observations originate from different sampling periods. The 1991–2020 period discussed in the associated manuscript refers to climatological environmental forcing used for flux reconstruction, rather than a common observation period for all records in this workbook. This deposit provides the observational compilation. Any reconstruction code, gridded flux products, or additional model outputs should be documented separately if included in this or a related deposit. Please acknowledge the original data sources when reusing individual observations.
title: GOcean-CH4: A global marine methane observation database supporting "Global Ocean Methane Database Construction and Interface Flux Reconstruction"

summary: Threading a flux through a ring often shifts its energy levels. In the N-site spin-one Motzkin ring, a boundary flux leaves the entire zero-magnetization spectrum unchanged, yet increases the ground-state entanglement by giving each spin path a phase set by its lowest height. For equal halves and fixed nontrivial flux, the excess von Neumann entropy tends to approximately 1.581 nats, while the excess logarithmic negativity grows as 2 log log N + O(1). The limiting Schmidt weights come in pairs, allowing local operations that conserve each half's magnetization to extract a logical Bell pair with fidelity approaching one. The manuscript also examines controlled deformations and contrasts this response with suppression in a uniformly gapped neutral sector and with the energy response induced by an additional reverse pair-conversion process.
title: Flux-Enhanced Entanglement with an Unchanged Zero-Magnetization Spectrum in a Motzkin Ring

summary: hPartition is a partitioning framework implemented natively inside IQ-TREE 2, which builds a partitioning scheme from site rates rather than from predefined gene or codon boundaries, and does so at a fraction of the time and memory that wrapper-based methods need. ✨ Key Features Native IQ-TREE 2 Integration: Implemented directly in C++ within the IQ-TREE 2 engine. Model fitting, site-wise likelihood evaluation and reassignment share one process and one in-memory alignment, and the framework inherits the engine's alignment and state-space handling rather than reimplementing it. Hybrid Partitioning Strategy: Model-free evolutionary rate estimation via a generalized fastTIGER , then seed binning, candidate-model selection, likelihood-based site reassignment, and a cleanup pass over undersized subsets. Data Types: Benchmarked on nucleotide and amino-acid alignments, and verified to run unchanged on binary data. Codon and morphological data are untested. Invariant Site Handling: Invariant sites are carried through the pipeline at rate zero and settled by likelihood-proportional sampling, so they disperse across the scheme instead of collecting in one zero-variance cluster. Small entirely invariant subsets still occur — in five of the eight DNA schemes examined — but no subset holds more than 11.8% of an alignment's invariant sites. hPartition-PF: An extended variant ( -hPartition-pf ) that passes the scheme to IQ-TREE's relaxed-clustering merge search. It produces markedly smaller schemes on every DNA dataset tested, at three to fourteen times the runtime, and improves BIC on 11 of 17. 📊 Benchmark Results Model fit: Lowest BIC of the methods compared on 16 of 17 empirical DNA alignments, 10 of 12 protein alignments, and three of four multi-locus alignments containing ribosomal or transfer RNA. Topological accuracy: On 100 simulated alignments per dataset, hPartition recovers a closer tree than gPartition on 56 and than PsiPartition on 66 (SimDNA1), and on 70 and 85 respectively (SimDNA2); all four comparisons are significant under a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The advantage is consistent rather than concentrated, but it is not universal. Speed: Against the fastest competitor on each alignment, 1.0–6.4× lower wall-clock time on DNA and 2.4–25.7× on protein. Scalability: Completes alignments on which the alternatives exceed a 10 GB memory allocation. 🧪 Benchmark Scripts & Reproducibility The scripts that produced every experiment in the manuscript are in hPartition_scripts/ , with revision/ holding those added during review (the RNA benchmark, the matched-model-set comparison, the Stage-2 ablation and the binary-data check). hPartition_scripts/README.md documents the two clusters the work ran on, how to point the scripts at your own binaries, and what each one produces. 🚀 Usage To partition an alignment with standard hPartition : iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -mset JC69,F81,HKY,GTR -hPartition # DNA iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -hPartition # protein For the merging extension hPartition-PF , append -pf : iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -mset JC69,F81,HKY,GTR -hPartition-pf # DNA The criterion defaults to BIC; --AIC and --AICc select the others. The scheme depends on the random seed and on the thread count, so hold both fixed within an analysis: every result reported in the manuscript was obtained at -seed 0 and one thread. 🛠️ Compilation from Source Pre-compiled binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows are in the assets below. To compile from source: ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Do not use the "Source code (zip)" or "Source code (tar.gz)" links GitHub generates at the bottom of this page — they omit the required Git submodules. Download the iqtree-...-source-with-submodules archive from the assets instead. Requirements (Linux): A C++ compiler (GCC >= 4.8, Clang, or Intel C++) CMake >= 2.8.10 Boost, Eigen3 and OpenMP (e.g. sudo apt-get install libboost-dev libeigen3-dev ) # 1. Extract the source archive and enter the directory
title: SliferSkyd/iqtree2: hPartition: An Efficient and Robust Alignment Partitioning Framework for Large-Scale DNA and Protein Phylogenomics

summary: Context: Software systems operating in regulated domains must often be adapted as legal and regulatory requirements evolve. While identifying regulatory changes is an important first step, determining which parts of a software repository are affected remains largely manual and knowledge-intensive. Objectives: This paper investigates how regulatory changes can be systematically mapped to affected parts of software repositories, and how this analysis can be supported through an evidence-grounded tool. Method: Following a Design Science Research approach, we conducted a multi-stage empirical investigation in collaboration with an industrial partner. We first developed a category-driven impact model linking regulatory change categories to potentially affected repository artifact types and engineering consequences. The model was then validated and refined with practitioners. Based on these findings, we designed and implemented ReguLens, which was subsequently examined through a formative expert evaluation and refined accordingly. The resulting version was evaluated using a controlled benchmark of 25 historical cases from three regulation-dependent open-source repositories. Results:  Practitioner validation showed that regulatory change categories provide useful structure for reasoning about likely software consequences, but should be treated as contextual guidance rather than deterministic mappings. The formative expert evaluation indicated that ReguLens can support exploration of potentially affected artifacts while still requiring expert interpretation. This observation was reinforced by the benchmark evaluation: ReguLens achieved 99.3% F1-score and 96.0% balanced accuracy for repository-level impact detection, whereas artifact localization was more challenging. For directly affected artifacts, macro F1 reached 64.1% at file level and 60.6% at container level, but decreased to 21.1% at symbol level. Conclusion:  Practitioners can benefit from ReguLens by using it to narrow the search space, identify plausible implementation entry points, and inspect supporting repository evidence. However, incomplete localization shows that human review remains necessary to interpret the evidence and confirm the required software changes. The findings therefore highlight both the potential and the current limitations of AI- assisted support for regulatory impact analysis.
title: Regulatory Impact Analysis in Software Repositories: From Category-Driven Modeling to Evidence-Grounded Tool Support

summary: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination

summary: Ensuring the provenance and authenticity of raw herbal materials in B2B supply chains requires integrating rapid species verification with immutable record-keeping. Existing centralized systems suffer from single-point trust vulnerability, while public blockchain architectures incur high gas fees and execution delays. This paper presents AyurAuth, a unified framework combining lightweight Edge-AI species classification using fine-tuned MobileNetV2 with a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric v2.x blockchain ledger. Deployed via a Node.js REST API and Flask microservice, AyurAuth achieves an empirical top-1 leaf classification accuracy of 85.00% (88.6 ms inference latency) across five key Ayurvedic herb species. Benchmark testing via Hyperledger Caliper demonstrates a peak write throughput of 408.47 TPS with a commit latency of 145.8 ms at 100 TPS, and a read throughput of 485.44 TPS at 41.5 ms latency with 100% success rate. End-to-end batch onboarding completes in 394.4 ms, while buyer QR verification queries execute in 28.5 ms without exposing internal ledger credentials.
title: AyurAuth: A Decentralized Edge-AI and Permissioned Blockchain Framework for Herbal Supply Chain Authenticity

summary: Abstract Modern websites frequently depend on multi-layer dynamic software stacks comprising application runtimes, content-management systems, databases, frameworks, authentication services, third-party APIs, and cloud infrastructure. This architecture provides substantial functionality under normal conditions but can produce an undesirable failure mode: essential public information may become inaccessible even when networking, HTTPS, web servers, and the ability to serve static files remain operational. This paper introduces Web Lifeboat, an experimental architecture and protocol for cryptographically verifiable static fallback publishing. The design seeks to preserve a small, explicitly selected set of essential web information independently of the normal dynamic application stack. Emergency content is represented as static HTML accompanied by a signed manifest describing its identity, integrity, validity period, sequence, and associated trust information. Verification is designed to require neither the site’s database nor its application runtime and to remain meaningful when content is transferred through different transports. Web Lifeboat applies principles of graceful degradation and cyber resilience to web publishing: failure of high-complexity functionality should not necessarily imply failure of low-complexity, mission-essential information delivery. The current protocol draft, version 1.5.2, defines deterministic validation semantics, resource limits, rollback protections, cryptographic verification, key-state handling, clock-uncertainty behaviour, and transition rules. An internal conformance suite contains 42 package and trust-transition cases. The suite currently passes both its own validation process and a separate Go implementation from the same development lineage; genuinely independent implementation testing remains pending. In addition to the protocol design, this work introduces a measurable availability criterion, the Essential Information Preservation Ratio (EIPR), and reports a controlled local PHP-runtime failure experiment. Version 1.1.0 supplies six figure sources and previews, all controlled benchmark observations and tables, four frozen BBBD EEG analysis inputs with time maps and saved FP64 outputs, and a complete Sherlock angular-gyrus fMRI application for the group response and 16 participants. Includes 17 segmentations, state-count curves, boundary-alignment and circular-shift statistics, source provenance, public acquisition/rerun scripts, and the current author manuscript with Online Resource 1. Algorithm software remains independently versioned as HP-GSBS 0.2.0. Original code is MIT; source data and applicable derived materials retain CC BY 4.0 attribution; see LICENSE, LICENSE-DATA, DATA_SOURCES.md and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

summary: A falsifiable, typed model separates ontological categories, epistemic states, evidence, consensus, uncertainty, provenance, and authority. The proposed protocol forbids consensus-only promotion of physical claims and requires traceable evidence for changes in verification status. Novelty and empirical advantage remain unestablished. The record also includes EM-001, a 100-case synthetic pilot (20 per domain: physics, medicine, finance, law, subjective experience) comparing majority vote, evidence-weighted scoring and RKCS. Illustrative synthetic accuracy: majority 0.30, evidence-weighted 0.70, RKCS 0.94 — labels are rule-derived and RKCS is scored against an oracle aligned with its own rules (circularity risk), so this is a software smoke test, not a performance claim. Preregistration draft NOT REGISTERED; human adjudication NOT RUN. Status: frozen proposed specification plus deterministic reference checker (7/7 synthetic unit tests pass), 2026-10-20; AI-assisted formulation. Source: the author's iCloud Recents (files dated 2026-10-21), downloaded 2026-10-22; published on Zenodo per the author's standing approval to publish all of his research, including items marked confidential/proprietary. The PDF was compiled with pdflatex from the package's unmodified main.tex (no PDF existed). The v0.1 package ZIP is also contained inside the EM-001 ZIP (folder rkcs_v0_1/ ); both original ZIPs are deposited. IETF status: converted by the author's assistant into the RFCXML v3 Internet-Draft draft-watts-reality-knowledge-consensus-separation-00 (intended status Informational), validated with xml2rfc 3.34.1 (no errors or warnings) and idnits 3 (0 errors, 0 warnings; 1 comment for the non-ASCII author name). Submitted to the IETF Datatracker on 2026-10-22 as submission 170763 ( status ); it is awaiting the author's email confirmation and is not posted until confirmed. Internet-Drafts are works in progress, not IETF standards. The I-D text is a faithful conversion of the paper (math rendered as plain text; the figure described in prose); the confidentiality handling label was left out of the I-D because it cannot carry one under BCP 78, and IANA/Security Considerations sections were added. License: the research package's own LICENSE file is retained unchanged (it carries the author's 'CONFIDENTIAL — PROPRIETARY' handling label and reserves rights; the author has since approved open publication). No Creative Commons license is granted; the Zenodo license field ('other open') refers to these terms. The attached Internet-Draft files ( .xml , .txt , .pdf named draft-watts-* ) are subject to BCP 78 and the IETF Trust's Legal Provisions Relating to IETF Documents ( https://trustee.ietf.org/license-info ). summary: This database compiles 263 flexural specimens with unbonded post-tensioning tendons from 27 published sources, covering simply supported (170) and continuous (93) members with internal (195) and external (68) tendons under single-point (98), two-point (90), and uniformly distributed (75) loading. For each specimen, it provides the tendon stress increment at ultimate (Δf_ps = f_ps − f_se) reported in the source, the effective prestress and tendon stress at ultimate, the basic member geometry, reinforcement, and material properties, and the non-dimensional input descriptors used to train the probabilistic Deep Gaussian process (DeepGP) surrogate model in the main paper. The values in the columns highlighted in blue (inputs) and orange (target) on the "Database" sheet are identical to the training dataset of the main paper and may be used to reproduce or benchmark data-driven prediction models. Please note that, to complete the dataset for model training, some parameters that were not explicitly reported in the original publications may have been estimated from figures, drawings, or common design practice; users are therefore kindly encouraged to consult the original sources listed below before using individual specimen data for detailed analysis.
title: Database of Tendon Stress Increments at Ultimate in Unbonded Post-Tensioned Concrete Members

summary: Replication package for "Integration without crossing: Artificial intelligence and the organisation of research across disciplines" (Sung-Jong Lee, submitted to Quantitative Science Studies). The study uses OpenAlex works (CC0) published in 2020–2025 by authors in 22 university departments, identified from raw affiliation strings. It tests whether AI is dissolving disciplinary boundaries, forming a discipline of its own, or being absorbed by existing disciplines, and replicates the department-based Correlation Matrix of Major Disciplines of Schwartz, Park & Lee (2016). Contents: - code/: Python scripts for sampling and downloading works, text representations (TF-IDF, MiniLM, SPECTER2), alignment and crossing measures, AI absorption, third-layer fields, the 2016 CMMD replication, alternative AI definitions, and all figures. - data/sample_work_ids.csv: OpenAlex IDs, publication years and department codes of all sampled works. Titles and abstracts can be retrieved from OpenAlex. - data/analysis/: derived tables behind every table and figure in the paper. Paper-level score files and embeddings are not included because they can be regenerated with the code. - README.md: pipeline steps and run commands. - MANIFEST.csv: file list with sizes and SHA-256 checksums. Licences: derived data under CC BY 4.0; code under the MIT License (LICENSE-CODE.txt).
