summary: This package contains the data and Python code needed to reproduce every table and figure in Holgersson and Brown, “Recognition Without Implementation: Property-Rights Compensation, Sámi Rights, and Felling Applications in Sweden’s Mountain-Adjacent Forests after Girjas” (manuscript JFE-06-2026-0002, Journal of Forest Economics). The paper examines applications for permits to fell mountain-adjacent forest (fjällnära skog) in Sweden, which lies wholly within the reindeer husbandry area, around two 2020 court rulings: the Supreme Court’s Girjas judgment of 23 January 2020 (NJA 2020 s. 3), which recognised Sámi customary hunting and fishing rights, and the Land and Environment Court of Appeal’s judgment of 12 May 2020 (MÖD 2020:8), which established that owners refused a felling permit are entitled to compensation from the state. The analysis compares annual, monthly, county and municipal data on felling applications and notifications, and data on compensation paid for refused permits, to separate the effects of the two rulings. Data. All data are official statistics from the Swedish Forest Agency (Skogsstyrelsen), downloaded from its statistical database in October 2026 or supplied by its Statistics Unit: JO031402b.xlsx: applications for permits for regeneration felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by region and ownership category, 1995–2024 (number and hectares). JO031406.xlsx: applications for permits in mountain-adjacent forest, national, by month, 2008–2026. JO031401b.xlsx: notifications of regeneration felling, by county and ownership category, 1995–2025. These exclude the mountain-adjacent permit applications. JO031412.xlsx: notifications and applications for regeneration felling, by municipality and ownership category, 2010–2025. JO031405.xlsx: area notified or applied for, by county and month, 2007–2026. compensation_JO_table07.csv: compensation (intrångsersättning) paid for refused felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by county, 2020–2025 (number, SEK and hectares). This was transcribed from Skogsstyrelsen’s table “Intrångsersättning för nekad avverkning i fjällnära skog per län” (formal protection and compensation, table 07). Values shown as “..” in the source are suppressed for confidentiality. Code (Python 3). Run python run_all.py . It executes the scripts below in order and writes all results to the same folder: analysis.py: national and county results by ownership category, decomposition into number and size of applications, structural-break scan and Figure 1 (Tables 2 and 3). monthly.py: monthly comparison around the two rulings and Figure 2. parse_extra.py: reads the county, municipal and monthly notification tables. comparison.py: comparisons with ordinary felling in the reindeer husbandry area, including difference-in-differences estimates (Table 4). eventstudy.py: county–ownership pair estimates and Figure 3. compensation.py: compensation paid compared with area applied for (Table 5). Requirements: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy, statsmodels and openpyxl. All are pre-installed in Google Colab. Notes on derived series. Västerbotten is calculated as Norra Norrland minus Norrbotten. Mountain-adjacent forest in Södra Norrland lies in Jämtland. Dalarna is the national total minus Norra Norrland and Södra Norrland. National area for individual owners in 2024 is suppressed in the source and recovered as all owners minus other owners. Version note. This version replaces version 1 (10.5281/zenodo.17249309), which accompanied an earlier draft of the paper. All results in the revised paper were recomputed from the official source tables included here, and version 1 should no longer be used.

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.

summary: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20 Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements? This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model. A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage. The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement. The proposed minimum experimental prototype uses a closed microfluidic chip with interchangeable handling modules, two independently referenced readout channels, simulated or inert-tracer specimens, a separate audit service, and a physically verifiable stop mechanism. Proposed tests include unauthorized-action challenges, hidden calibration drift, interrupted events, sample contamination, unannounced network partitions, and independent laboratory replay or rerun. DOI-linked scientific references establish the relevant literature in automated laboratories, microrobotics, quantum sensing, uncertainty metrology, FAIR data stewardship, and computational reproducibility. They do not independently validate the integrated system proposed here. SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This book is a hypothesis-forming nonclinical research architecture. It reports no completed microrobotic or quantum biosensing experiments, no demonstrated clinical performance, no universal quantum advantage, and no autonomous system capable of authorizing itself. Statistical models, formulas, and decision policies require experimental verification, specialized review, and appropriate boundary conditions. A failed external reference, unavailable provenance chain, or revoked permission requires abstention rather than inference by convenience. STARLI RESEARCH PHILOSOPHY A trustworthy laboratory must remain answerable to evidence outside itself. Autonomy becomes scientifically meaningful when an experiment can be stopped, questioned, reconstructed, and handed to future researchers who retain the right to refuse its original assumptions.
